meta.description: Not Seneca. It is an anonymous English proverb in print by 1850; the Seneca credit first appears in a 1955 Louisiana newspaper column.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There Is No Right Way to Do the Wrong Thing'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Seneca. An anonymous proverb in print by 1850, credited to Seneca only from 1955 — and later to Waylon Jennings and Toby Keith.

answer.label: Not Seneca — an anonymous English proverb
answer.sourceLine: This is a proverb with no known author, not a line from Seneca. The earliest appearance Quote Investigator documents is an 1850 essay on British rule in India in De Bow’s Southern and Western Review — “There is no right way of doing a wrong thing” — and the Seneca credit does not surface until a Baton Rouge newspaper column in 1955.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: De Bow’s Southern and Western Review, July 1850
Charles Jewett: Life and Recollections (1880), p. 411
First documented 1955, in a Baton Rouge newspaper column

source.excerpt: A man may do a right thing in a wrong way; but he cannot do a wrong thing in a right way. For there is no right way of doing wrong. If there were, it is a question whether he would not be as badly off in doing right in a wrong way, as he would be in doing wrong in a right way.
trail: 1850 — the oldest appearance on record. An essay on British rule in India by “W. Adam, Esq.” in De Bow’s Southern and Western Review argues that “There is no right way of doing a wrong thing; and while the relation itself is allowed to continue, the mode of acting under that relation must partake of its vicious and unnatural character,” as documented by Quote Investigator ↗.

1880 — the temperance lecturer Charles Jewett is quoted saying “he cannot do a wrong thing in a right way. For there is no right way of doing wrong,” on page 411 of Charles Jewett: Life and Recollections ↗ — a scan anyone can read today.

1955 — the first Seneca credit anyone has found: a Baton Rouge column presents it as something “the ancient Roman philosopher, Seneca,” said, more than a century after the proverb was already circulating, traced by Quote Investigator ↗.

1974–2006 — the modern wording takes hold: a 1974 Connecticut newspaper filler about Washington, Dick Armey handing it to Waylon Jennings in 1996, and finally Toby Keith’s “Ain’t No Right Way” on White Trash with Money ↗ in 2006.
source.excerptNote: Charles Jewett, the temperance campaigner, in the “Table Talk” chapter of William M. Thayer’s 1880 biography. This is the nineteenth-century shape of the saying — “a wrong thing,” spelled out at length. The clipped modern catchphrase, with “the wrong thing,” turns up much later in Quote Investigator’s citation record.

source.rightsNote: No rights status can be asserted for the quotation itself: it is an anonymous proverb with no identified author and no identifiable first work, and the exact modern wording cannot be tied to any specific publication. Nothing shown on this page is encumbered — the 1850 periodical and the 1880 biography excerpted above are long out of copyright in the United States — but that says nothing about the saying, which nobody has ever been shown to own.

author.name: Seneca the Younger
author.kicker: The name it gets pinned on
author.heading: Why Seneca?
author.metaLine: c. 4 BC – AD 65 · Roman Stoic philosopher, dramatist and statesman
author.bio: Lucius Annaeus Seneca the Younger was a Stoic philosopher, tragedian and Roman statesman who served as tutor and then adviser to the emperor Nero. His surviving work — the Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium, a dozen ethical essays, the Naturales Quaestiones and nine tragedies — is one of the largest bodies of ancient Stoic writing we still have, which is exactly why unsourced moral one-liners drift toward his name. This particular sentence is not among them: it appears nowhere in the sourced sections of his Wikiquote page, and the proverb is first recorded in English in the nineteenth century, nearly eighteen centuries after his death.

misattribution.heading: Who else gets the credit
misattribution.intro: An ownerless proverb attracts owners. At least four names have been attached to this one, and the paper trail shows every one of them arriving long after the saying was already in print.

items.why: The earliest Seneca credit on record is a “Pull Up A Chair” column in the State Times Advocate of Baton Rouge on 6 May 1955, which introduced it as something “the ancient Roman philosopher, Seneca, said,” per Quote Investigator ↗. That is more than a century after the saying was already in American print, and the line appears nowhere in Wikiquote’s Seneca collection ↗.
In April 1996 the congressman Dick Armey told the Dallas Morning News, “Waylon Jennings has a great line: ‘There ain’t no right way to do the wrong thing,’” as recorded by Quote Investigator ↗.

“Ain’t No Right Way,” written with Scotty Emerick and Dean Dillon, is track 9 on White Trash with Money ↗, released 11 April 2006 — the chorus uses a proverb roughly a century and a half older than the record.

Goodreads files “There is no right way to do a wrong thing” under Kushner’s Living a Life That Matters ↗, which is where a great many readers first meet it — but the wording predates the book by generations.

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator ↗ concludes that the aphorism was in circulation by 1850 and that Anonymous is the reasonable attribution — and reports that the compilers of The Dictionary of Modern Proverbs, having found a citation before 1900, moved it to their appendix of “No Longer Modern Proverbs.”

context.heading: A proverb with a very long career
lead: Some misattributions are inventions. This one is a genuine saying that simply never had an owner. It surfaces in American and British print through the second half of the nineteenth century in a cluster of near-identical shapes — an 1850 argument against British rule in India, an 1880 temperance lecture, an 1891 newspaper filler credited only to another paper, an 1898 church magazine — which is exactly what a proverb in circulation looks like. Nobody coined it on the record; it was already common property.

Because it has no author, it has been handed to a lot of people. A 1955 Louisiana columnist gave it to Seneca. A congressman gave it to Waylon Jennings in 1996. Toby Keith put it in a song chorus in 2006. Each of those is a person repeating a line that was already a century or more old when they got to it.
detailsBody: The nineteenth-century printings say “a wrong thing”; the modern catchphrase says “the wrong thing.” Quote Investigator’s citation record shows that definite-article form arriving late — in a 1974 Connecticut newspaper “Today’s Chuckle” item aimed at Washington. Proverbs behave like this: they get smoothed, shortened and re-pointed at whatever the speaker is annoyed about, which is one reason no single printed instance can be called the original.

The Dictionary of Modern Proverbs (Yale University Press, 2012), compiled by Charles Clay Doyle, Wolfgang Mieder and Fred R. Shapiro, initially treated the saying as a twentieth-century coinage. Quote Investigator reports that the compilers found a citation before 1900 and moved it into the book’s appendix of “No Longer Modern Proverbs.”
context.pull: It was never Seneca’s to lose — it was already everybody’s.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator dates the aphorism to print by 1850 (W. Adam in De Bow's Southern and Western Review, July 1850), lists 1880, 1891, 1898, 1947, 1974 and 1996 citations, records the first Seneca credit in the State Times Advocate of Baton Rouge on 6 May 1955, records Dick Armey crediting Waylon Jennings in the Dallas Morning News in April 1996, notes The Dictionary of Modern Proverbs moved it to an appendix of 'No Longer Modern Proverbs', and concludes Anonymous is a reasonable attribution.

The 1880 book Charles Jewett: Life and Recollections by William M. Thayer (Boston, J. H. Earle) contains, on page 411, 'A man may do a right thing in a wrong way; but he cannot do a wrong thing in a right way. For there is no right way of doing wrong...' — verified in the item's full text on the Internet Archive.
Wikiquote's Seneca the Younger page does not list 'There is no right way to do a wrong thing' or 'no right way to do the wrong thing' in any section, sourced, disputed or misattributed.

Seneca the Younger lived c. 4 BC – AD 65 and was a Roman Stoic philosopher, statesman and dramatist who tutored and later advised Nero; his surviving works include the Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium, twelve ethical essays, the Naturales Quaestiones and nine tragedies.
Toby Keith's album White Trash with Money was released 11 April 2006 and its track 9 is 'Ain't No Right Way', written by Toby Keith, Scotty Emerick and Dean Dillon.
Goodreads credits 'There is no right way to do a wrong thing.' to Harold S. Kushner, Living a Life That Matters: Resolving the Conflict Between Conscience and Success.
The Dictionary of Modern Proverbs was compiled by Charles Clay Doyle, Wolfgang Mieder and Fred R. Shapiro and published by Yale University Press in 2012.
